hello.note: Polite, for anyone. The reply is وعليكم السلام (wa a-LEY-kum is-sa-LAAM). Friends say أهلاً (AH-lan), hi

how-are-you.note: Said to a man. To a woman, the end is said iz-ZAY-yik. Written the same

im-well.note: Literally "good, thank God", the usual answer whoever is asking

good-morning.note: The usual reply is صباح النور (sa-BAAH in-NUUR), morning of light

good-night.note: Said when parting at night, to a man. To a woman, tis-BA-hi a-la KHEER. Good evening is مساء الخير (ma-SAA il-KHEER)

goodbye.note: Literally "with safety", the same for anyone. Bye (baay) is common in Cairo too

please.note: Said to a man. To a woman, law sa-MAH-ti (لو سمحتي). It also gets a waiter's attention

thank-you.note: شكراً جزيلاً (SHUK-ran ga-ZEE-lan) means thank you very much

youre-welcome.note: Also heard: ولا يهمك (wa-la ye-HIM-mak), don't mention it

yes.note: The everyday Egyptian yes. نعم (NA-am) is the formal one

no.note: Add شكراً, la SHUK-ran, to turn down a seller kindly

excuse-me.note: Sorry. To get past someone or catch their attention, say لو سمحت (law sa-MAHT)

my-name.note: The same for a man or a woman. The audio uses Peter as the example name

your-name.note: حضرتك (had-RIT-ak), literally "your presence", is the polite you for a stranger. To a woman, had-RIT-ik. Written the same

where-from.note: To a woman, had-RIT-ik mi-NEEN. Written the same

its-beautiful.note: أوي (A-wi) means very, and goes after the word. In Egypt ج is a hard g

speak-slowly.note: Literally "gently a little, please", the same whoever you ask

speak-english.note: Literally "is there anyone who speaks English?", the same whoever you ask

hundred.note: Written like water, مية (MAY-ya), but said differently

thousand.note: Prices are in Egyptian pounds, جنيه (gi-NEEH): ألف جنيه is 1,000 pounds

how-much.note: Literally "for how much is this?" Point at the thing

would-like.note: Literally "is ... possible, please?", the polite way to order, the same for a man or a woman. The audio uses قهوة (AH-wa), a coffee, as the example

i-want.note: More direct than MUM-kin. The audio uses ده (da), this one, as the example

do-you-have.note: Literally "do you all have", the usual way to ask in a shop. The audio uses شاي (shaay), tea, as the example

just-looking.note: The same for a man or a woman. Useful in a market

ill-take-it.note: The same for a man or a woman

discount.note: Haggling is normal in markets such as Khan el-Khalili, not in shops with prices. آخر كلام؟ (AA-khir ka-LAAM), your last word?, asks for the final price

card.note: Literally "do you take Visa?", the usual way to ask about any card. Markets and taxis want cash

checkout-time.note: Egyptian Arabic borrows check-out from English

toilet.note: فين (FEEN) means where, and goes after the place

taxi.note: Said to a man. To a woman, tu-tlu-BI-li. Agree the fare first, or use an app

train.note: In Cairo ق is a catch in the throat, so قطر is said atr

bus-station.note: Also a bus stop. Long-distance buses leave from a موقف (MAW-if), a terminal

train-station.note: Cairo's main station is محطة مصر (ma-HAT-tit MASR), at Ramses Square

which-train.note: Literally "which train is going ...?" The audio uses إسكندرية (is-kin-de-REE-ya), Alexandria, as the example

buy-ticket.note: Literally "I buy a ticket from where?"

two-tickets.note: لـ (li) means to, and joins the front of the place. The audio uses Alexandria as the example

trip-length.note: The audio uses Alexandria as the example

delicious.note: حلو (HIL-w) means sweet, nice and tasty

allergic.note: Literally "I have an allergy to", the same for a man or a woman. Add the food: السمك (is-SA-mak) fish, المكسرات (il-mi-kas-sa-RAAT) nuts, البيض (il-BEED) eggs. The audio uses nuts

love-dish.note: Literally "this dish drives you crazy", a happy compliment the same for anyone

what-called.note: Point at the dish or item

table-for-two.note: For more people: لتلاتة (li-ta-LAA-ta), 3, or لأربعة (li-AR-ba-a), 4

recommend.note: Literally "what's the best thing you have?"

beer.note: Only some restaurants, bars and hotels serve alcohol. Stella is the local beer

coffee.note: Turkish-style coffee. Say how sweet: سادة (SAA-da) none, مظبوط (maz-BUUT) medium, زيادة (zi-YAA-da) sweet

tea.note: The national drink, strong and sweet. With mint: شاي بالنعناع (shaay bin-NI-naa)

water.note: Bottled water is مية معدنية (MAY-ya ma-da-NEE-ya)

hot.note: Hot to touch. Hot weather is حر (HARR). Spicy is حراق (har-RAA')

cold.note: Cold to touch, and cold drinks. Cold weather is برد (BARD)

cheers.note: Literally "to your health", to a man. To a woman, fi SIH-tik. Written the same

help.note: Shout it. The police are on 122

pharmacy.note: Pharmacies are everywhere, many open late, and the pharmacist often speaks some English
